items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: We followed, we were fortunate to follow Duke Ellington featuring Ella Fitzgerald in Southern France right at the edge of the Mediterranean

ctx.x: Well I’m not sure what I mean and I’m glad you asked that. It seems that the music had a reason for being other than just we have, you know we got a recording date, different from perhaps when a bop musician would get a date and they would get six or seven tunes together, some that they had written and some standards, where the music that you were involved in in the 60s seemed to have another level to it, that there was an intent to affect people as they listened.

Yes. That quality of expression for me began with the Charles Lloyd Quartet. It actually began, we were, I remember during our first performance in Antibes France, this is Jack DeJohnette, Keith Jarrett, myself and Charles Lloyd. We followed, we were fortunate to follow Duke Ellington featuring Ella Fitzgerald in Southern France right at the edge of the Mediterranean with maybe 3- 4,000 people seated outside sort of in an ampitheatrical set up there. We followed Duke Ellington featuring Ella Fitzgerald with the…

would sometimes come from a place that I don’t even know about. When I was a young man of course there was the church and there was the community where you heard music that made you, that called your attention to persons or groups that were feeling something. So the Charles Lloyd group was one that prepared me for that Alice Coltrane recording, because that “Journey in Satchidananda” meant that she was going there to pray, to respect the gods of her choice, you know, so far as being her continued existence…
